client: I've been having a really hard time since my younger sister passed away six months ago in a car accident. It's like everything that used to make me happy just feels hollow now, and I can't seem to find any joy in the things I used to love. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I had to try something.
therapist: I'm so deeply sorry for the loss of your sister — losing someone you love so suddenly and tragically is one of the most painful experiences a person can go through, and everything you're feeling makes complete sense. That hollowness you're describing, where things that once brought joy now feel empty, is a very real and common part of grief, and it doesn't mean joy is gone forever — just that it's been overshadowed by an enormous loss. I'm really glad you decided to try, and I want you to know this is a safe space to go at whatever pace feels right for you. What feels most heavy for you right now — is it the grief itself, the loss of those moments of joy, or something else entirely?

client: Honestly, what feels heaviest is the guilt. The last time I talked to her, we had this stupid argument over something I can't even remember now, and I never got the chance to fix it. I keep replaying that conversation over and over, thinking if I had just called her back sooner or been less stubborn, maybe things would have been different somehow.
therapist: That guilt you're carrying sounds absolutely exhausting — replaying that conversation over and over, searching for a way you could have changed things, is such a painful place to be stuck. I want to gently reflect something back to you: the argument you had was a normal, human moment between two people who loved each other, and it's worth asking whether your sister would truly want you to define your entire relationship by that one conversation. What do you think she would say if she could see the weight you've been carrying on her behalf?

client: I know in my head that she probably wouldn't want me to feel this way, and part of me thinks she'd tell me to stop being so hard on myself. But it's like knowing that doesn't actually make the feeling go away, you know? It's easy to say she would forgive me, but I can't hear her say it, and that's the part that's impossible to get past.
therapist: You've just touched on something really profound — there's a painful gap between what we *know* intellectually and what we can actually *feel* in our hearts, and grief makes that gap feel impossibly wide. The fact that you can't hear her voice saying those words is a real loss within the loss, and it makes complete sense that logic alone can't reach that hurt. I'm wondering — are there other ways she showed you, throughout your relationship, that she loved you and valued you beyond any single argument?

client: Yeah, there were a lot of those moments, actually. She used to call me just to tell me something funny that happened to her, even when it was late and she knew I had work the next day, because she said I was the only one who would really get the joke. But trying to hold onto those memories feels almost painful too, because they just remind me of everything I've lost and won't get back.
therapist: The fact that she called *you* — specifically you — because you were the one who would truly "get it," speaks volumes about the kind of bond you had, and that's something no argument could erase. It makes so much sense that those beautiful memories feel bittersweet right now, almost like touching something that's both precious and painful at the same time — that's actually a sign of how deep your love for her was. I'm curious, when you let yourself sit with one of those memories, like the late-night calls, do you notice any part of it that feels like connection to her still, even alongside the pain?

client: Maybe there's a tiny flicker of something like connection, but I feel almost guilty admitting that, like if I let myself feel close to her through those memories, I'm somehow accepting that she's really gone and that feels unbearable. It's easier in a way to stay stuck in the guilt because at least that feels like I'm still fighting against what happened, if that makes any sense. I don't know if I'm ready to let the memories be comforting instead of just painful.
therapist: What you just said takes real courage and self-awareness — you've identified something really important, that the guilt has actually been serving a purpose, keeping you in a kind of fight against the reality of losing her, which feels more bearable than acceptance. But I want to offer a gentle reframe: allowing yourself to feel that flicker of connection through memories isn't surrendering to her being gone — it's actually a way of keeping her *with* you, on your own terms. You don't have to be ready for that shift all at once, but I'm wondering — does staying in the guilt actually feel like it's keeping you closer to her, or does it sometimes feel like it's keeping you from her?

client: That question actually stopped me for a second, because honestly when I sit with it, the guilt does feel isolating, like I'm locked in this room with only the worst version of our last interaction and nothing else can get in. But I'm not sure I trust myself to just decide to shift toward the memories instead, because what if I start feeling better and then that feels like betraying her somehow, like I'm moving on too fast. I guess I'm scared that healing and losing her are the same thing.
therapist: What you just said — "healing and losing her are the same thing" — is one of the most honest and courageous things you could have named, and I think so many people who grieve carry that fear without ever finding words for it. But I want to sit with you in this gentle question: is it possible that healing isn't about losing her, but about slowly expanding that locked room so that *all* of her can be present with you — the late-night calls, the shared jokes, the whole relationship — not just that last argument? You get to define what moving forward looks like, and it doesn't have to mean leaving her behind — so what would healing look like to you if it *didn't* mean betraying her?

client: I've never really thought about it that way before, like healing could mean making room for all of her instead of just erasing the bad part or pretending it didn't happen. Maybe healing could look like being able to tell one of her jokes to someone else someday, or picking up the phone when I see something funny and then remembering I can't call her, but still feeling like she would have loved it. I don't know if I'm there yet, but that version of healing feels a little less terrifying than what I thought it had to be.
therapist: What you just described is genuinely beautiful — carrying her with you in those moments, seeing something funny and feeling her presence in your reaction to it, that *is* a form of connection that doesn't require letting go. The fact that this version of healing feels even a little less terrifying tells me that somewhere inside you, you're already moving toward it in your own quiet way. I want to ask — is there one small moment this week where you might let yourself share something with her in that way, even just privately, like noticing something she would have loved and allowing yourself to think "she would have gotten that"?

client: I think I could maybe try that, but I'm already worried that in the moment it'll just make me break down instead of feeling connected to her. Like, what if I notice something she would have loved and instead of it feeling warm, it just feels like a punch in the stomach all over again? I want to try, but I don't want to set myself up for a moment that just leaves me feeling worse and more alone than before.
therapist: That fear is completely valid, and it's actually wise to think ahead about how it might feel rather than just rushing in — both outcomes you're describing, the warmth *and* the punch in the stomach, might even happen at the same time, and that would be okay too. What matters isn't that the moment feels perfect, but that you're gentle with yourself whatever comes up — even breaking down could be a sign that you're letting her in, not that you've failed the experiment. I'm wondering, is there someone safe who could be nearby when you try this, so that if it does feel like a punch, you don't have to sit alone with it afterward?

client: That's actually the part that scares me almost as much as the moment itself, because I've kind of pulled away from most people since she died and I'm not sure who I would even call. I don't want to burden anyone, and honestly I've gotten so used to being alone with all of this that I'm not even sure I know how to let someone sit with me in it anymore. It feels like grief has made me lonelier, but reaching out feels just as hard as everything else right now.
therapist: The loneliness you're describing — feeling isolated by grief and then finding that reaching out feels almost impossible — is one of the cruelest parts of loss, and it makes complete sense that you've withdrawn when everything has felt so heavy and raw. I want to gently notice something though: you *did* reach out today, here, and you've been remarkably open and honest throughout our conversation, which tells me that part of you still knows how to let someone sit with you, even if it's rusty. I'm curious — is there even one person in your life, however distant things have felt lately, who you think might actually want to hear from you, even if you're not sure what you'd say?

client: There's one friend, Maya, who has texted me a few times since the funeral and I keep leaving her messages on read because I just don't know what to say. I guess part of me thinks if I respond now, after all this time, she'll either be hurt that I disappeared or she'll ask how I'm doing and I won't know how to answer without it turning into this whole heavy thing. But you pointing out that I reached out today actually made me think maybe I'm not as completely closed off as I thought I was.
therapist: Maya has texted you *multiple times* — that's someone who is still reaching toward you, and that kind of persistence usually means she's not waiting to judge you for the silence, but just hoping to hear that you're okay. And you've already shown today that you can let someone in without having to have the perfect words ready — you didn't know exactly what to say when you started this conversation either, but look how far you've come. I wonder — what if your response to Maya didn't have to explain everything, but could just be something small and honest, like "I've been struggling but I've been thinking of you" — does that feel like something that might be possible?
